cue: How do you say someone is thoroughly kind?

es.literal: to be a piece of bread
es.meaning: To be a thoroughly good-natured, harmless person.
es.example: Su abuela es un pedazo de pan: no le ha dicho que no a nadie en su vida.
es.exampleTranslation: His grandmother is an absolute sweetheart — she's never said no to anyone in her life.

it.literal: to be a piece of bread
it.meaning: To be a thoroughly good-natured, harmless person.
it.example: Tua nonna è un pezzo di pane: non ha mai detto di no a nessuno.
it.exampleTranslation: Your grandmother is an absolute sweetheart — she's never said no to anyone.

bridge.note: Bread as a measure of harmlessness, in both languages, down to the same odd choice of a PIECE of it rather than a loaf — pezzo and pedazo, the same word twice. Italian keeps a second way of saying it that Spanish did not build: buono come il pane, good as bread, which turns the metaphor into a simile. Spanish only has the metaphor. So the two languages agree on the image and differ on how many grammatical shapes they let it take.

interference.es_to_it: Both work in Italian, and they are not the same sentence: 'è un pezzo di pane' says he IS the bread, 'è buono come il pane' says he is LIKE it. A Spanish speaker who only knows the metaphor will not recognise the simile when it arrives.
interference.it_to_es: 'Bueno como el pan' is not the Spanish idiom — Spanish keeps the metaphor only, ser un pedazo de pan. Note the article: Spanish takes UN pedazo, Italian UN pezzo, both indefinite, which is the easy half of this pair.
